clinicalPearls: Caused by recessive variants in SGCA encoding alpha-sarcoglycan; it is the commonest of the four sarcoglycanopathies (LGMD R3-R6) in most populations.
Presentation is often in childhood with a Duchenne-like picture: proximal pelvic then shoulder-girdle weakness, calf hypertrophy, toe-walking and a positive Gowers manoeuvre.
Serum creatine kinase is typically greatly elevated, in the range seen with dystrophinopathies, reflecting active muscle breakdown.

Because loss of one sarcoglycan destabilises the whole complex, immunostaining frequently shows reduced labelling of all four sarcoglycans, so protein testing localises the complex but genetics identifies the specific subunit.
Cognition is preserved, which helps separate it clinically from Duchenne muscular dystrophy despite the overlapping motor picture.
Respiratory muscle weakness tends to develop as disease advances and warrants scheduled surveillance of ventilatory function.
Cardiac involvement occurs but is generally less prominent and less consistent than in beta- and delta-sarcoglycanopathy (LGMD R4 and R6).
reference.pathophysiology: LGMD R3 arises from biallelic pathogenic variants in SGCA on chromosome 17q21, encoding alpha-sarcoglycan, a transmembrane glycoprotein of the sarcoglycan subcomplex within the larger dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex at the sarcolemma. The sarcoglycans (alpha, beta, gamma, delta) assemble interdependently, so a pathogenic change in the alpha subunit destabilises and reduces membrane expression of the entire tetramer. This weakens the mechanical link between the intracellular cytoskeleton and the extracellular matrix, so contractile stress is transmitted poorly and the membrane becomes vulnerable to contraction-induced injury. The result is repeated cycles of fibre necrosis and regeneration with progressive fibrosis, closely mirroring the mechanism of dystrophinopathy and accounting for the Duchenne-like clinical and biochemical picture.
additionalDifferentials: Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy (dystrophinopathy) given the overlapping childhood proximal phenotype
additionalInvestigations: Muscle biopsy with immunohistochemistry for all four sarcoglycans and for dystrophin to exclude dystrophinopathy
Immunoblot to quantify sarcoglycan complex reduction
Targeted SGCA sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, or an LGMD gene panel covering all sarcoglycans
Baseline and surveillance echocardiography and electrocardiography
Pulmonary function testing including seated and supine spirometry
redFlags: Loss of independent ambulation in later childhood or adolescence
Symptoms or signs of nocturnal hypoventilation such as morning headache and daytime somnolence
New cardiac symptoms or conduction changes on electrocardiography
Perioperative anaesthetic risk related to reduced respiratory reserve
reference.prognosis: Untreated, many patients lose independent walking during the second decade, with the pace influenced by the severity of the underlying variants. Long-term outlook depends chiefly on respiratory muscle involvement and, less consistently than in beta- or delta-subtypes, on cardiac status.
pitfalls: Assuming the diagnosis is Duchenne muscular dystrophy in a boy and stopping the workup once dystrophin looks borderline
Reading reduced staining of all sarcoglycans as pointing to a single subtype without confirmatory genetics
Underestimating respiratory decline because limb weakness appears to have plateaued
Overlooking female patients because the pattern superficially resembles X-linked dystrophinopathy
references: Peer-reviewed limb-girdle muscular dystrophy classification and consensus statements
Muscular dystrophy cardiac and respiratory surveillance guidelines
management: No disease-specific pharmacotherapy is available; care is supportive and delivered through a specialist neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maintain function, prevent contractures and provide orthoses, walking aids and wheelchair provision as ambulation declines
Scheduled respiratory surveillance with seated and supine spirometry, introducing non-invasive ventilation for nocturnal hypoventilation
Cardiac surveillance with echocardiography and ECG, treating any cardiomyopathy with standard heart-failure therapy such as ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers
Orthopaedic and spinal monitoring for scoliosis and contractures, with corrective surgery where indicated
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance
Escalate to assisted ventilation and structured palliative and respiratory support as ventilatory failure develops
